questions.q: Why does modern JavaScript favor let and const over var?
choices: var was removed from the language
let and const fixed confusing edge cases var had around scope
var only works on servers
let and const run faster in every case
questions.explanation: var still works, but its scoping rules produced confusing bugs. let and const fixed those edge cases, which is why modern code uses them almost exclusively — const for values that won't be reassigned, let for values that will.

questions.q: What's the main risk of using == instead of === in JavaScript?
choices: == is slower to type
== silently converts types before comparing, which can produce surprising results
== only works with numbers
== is deprecated and throws an error
questions.explanation: == performs implicit type conversion before comparing, so "5" == 5 is true. === compares value and type together with no conversion, which avoids that entire class of bug.

choices: Creates a new element with the id counter
Finds and returns the first element matching that CSS selector
Deletes the element with that id
Counts how many elements match that selector
questions.explanation: querySelector finds the first element matching a CSS selector and returns it so your code can read or change it. It doesn't create, delete, or count elements.

questions.q: In the event → listener → DOM update → redraw loop, what triggers the listener function to run?
choices: The page finishing its initial load
An event, such as a click, that the element is listening for
A fixed timer that runs every second
The browser refreshing automatically
questions.explanation: addEventListener registers a callback that runs whenever the specified event fires on that element — a click, an input change, a form submit, and so on. Nothing runs until the event actually happens.

choices: Only in the browser
Only on a server, via Node.js
In the browser, and — as covered in Lesson 7 — on servers too
Only inside a database
questions.explanation: JavaScript was originally browser-only, but today it also runs on servers via Node.js (Lesson 7). That's what "full stack JavaScript" means — one language front to back.
